newsitem.title: USA: Bob Dole leads drive for World War Two monument.
newsitem.headline: Bob Dole leads drive for World War Two monument.

text.p: Fifty-two years after a German shell nearly tore off his right arm and shoulder, former Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole on Wednesday took on the new mission of remembering fellow Americans who fought during World War Two.

The 73-year-old former Senate Republican leader, who lost his presidential bid to President Bill Clinton in November, accepted his first post-election job as co-chairman of a drive to build a World War Two Memorial on Washington's famed mall between the Lincoln Memorial and the Washington Monument.

While Washington's many monuments include memorials to Vietnam War and Korean War veterans and to those killed in all wars whose remains are unidentified, none specifically honour the 16 million Americans who served in the last world war.
Dole said in remarks prepared for a ceremony at the mall that he was honoured to serve in his new role to help raise $100 million to build the memorial.

"World War Two has been called 'the good war'," Dole said. "But there is nothing good about war for those who have known the heat and hate and horror of battle. Only causes can be good. And in this war we found a cause to justify the greatest sacrifice."
That cause, he said, was a fight against aggression. "We came to know we were fighting against evil."

Dole, a decorated platoon leader with the 10th Mountain Division, still bears pain from the day in April 1945 when German gunners nearly killed him on a hill in Italy. He was left with a useless right arm.

"The tank jacket was shredded open near the neck and shoulder," wrote biographer Richard Ben Cramer. "You could see into Dole through the jacket, through the shoulder, like a gouged fruit, see down to the core..."
In his remarks, Dole said the war was long ago but in his mind, and the minds of combat colleagues, it was like yesterday.
"World War Two is one of those rare events in history that look even larger from a distance," Dole said.

"But for those who served, we did not see the big picture, we saw the small struggles. We did not hear the call of history, we heard the voices of friends. Voices that still haunt and comfort the memory of veterans. Voices of confidence. Voices of fear. Voices that ended in a moment, in a place far from home.
"I can hear them as if it were yesterday, frozen in time by the intensity of the experience we shared. Forever bold. Forever determined. Forever young."
He said the monument, authorised by Congress in 1993, will honour all those "who liberated whole continents from tyranny, armed with courage and stainless patriotism."

Dole's co-chairman in the effort to raise funds -- who officials said would be a corporate leader -- has not been named. The memorial, designed by Friedrich St. Florian, a former dean of the Rhode Island School of Design, will be funded by private, corporate and foundation dollars.
Clinton dedicated the 7.4-acre (three-hectare) site on Veterans Day two years ago, but the location has become the subject of controversy.
Critics complain it will interfere with the great view between the monuments honouring former presidents George Washington and Abraham Lincoln.

Among the critics are Nebraska Democratic Sen. Bob Kerrey, who has asked the American Battle Monuments Commission to find another site. Kerrey lost a leg during the Vietnam War and holds the nation's highest military honour for valour, the Congressional Medal of Honour.
